title: the family word he chose

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunday, the gift inside the obligation. Your line was: one day that isn't yours to fill. And that's two weeks. This week: Francis, candles, the beads, the Hail Mary, confession, Sunday. Day fourteen.
screen: `ONE DAY THAT ISN'T YOURS TO FILL.` → `TWO WEEKS.`

segments.voice: Think about how you address people. Your boss gets your best email voice. A judge gets your honor. A king, in the old days, got your majesty, said from your knees. The more powerful someone is, the more careful and formal the words. Now imagine a group of friends asking their teacher: teach us to pray. How do you talk to the one who made the stars? You'd expect titles. A long list of them. Instead he gives them a prayer that begins with the word a child uses at the kitchen table. You've heard this prayer at the start of every decade of the rosary. Today, the family word he chose.
screen: `YOUR HONOR. YOUR MAJESTY.` → `TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `A WORD FROM THE KITCHEN TABLE.`

segments.voice: In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, it starts: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." Father. Behind the Greek of the Gospels, most scholars hear the Aramaic word Jesus spoke at home: abba. Mark's Gospel keeps that word untranslated, on the night before he died, when Jesus prays in the garden: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee." Abba is the word a son or daughter uses. Not a title. A relationship. And then look at the word before it: our. Not my Father. Our. Catholics notice that there isn't a single I or me in the whole prayer. Give us. Forgive us. Lead us. Deliver us. Even alone in your room at night, you pray it in the plural, standing in a crowd you can't see. That's the family word doing its work twice: God is not a stranger, and neither is the person next to you. Remember the handshake from day four? In the Mass, the whole room prays the Our Father together right before it. Catholics call it the Lord's Prayer too, and for centuries they prayed it in Latin: Pater noster, our Father. You might notice one difference if you visit other churches. Many Protestants end with, for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. In Matthew's oldest manuscripts that line isn't there, and Catholics usually stop at deliver us from evil. At Mass, the priest adds a short prayer, and then everyone says a version of it together. Same prayer, two old habits. And it opens with a family word.
screen: `ABBA — FATHER, AT HOME.` · `OUR, NOT MY.` · `NO I, NO ME.` · `PATER NOSTER.` · then, large: `NOT A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for the end of week two. A forty-five-second sit. Say just the first two words, slowly, out loud or silently: our Father. On our, think of someone you'd rather not include in that word, and include them anyway. On Father, notice how different it feels from a title. If you pray the whole prayer, you can pray it once, very slowly. The bell holds the time.
The Our Father. The prayer Jesus taught, opening with a family word, and with no I or me in it anywhere. Fourteenth word.
Your line: not a stranger. Today, treat one stranger like family for a moment: a name, a thank-you, a question about their day. Day fourteen. Two weeks.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Our Father at every Mass, standing together before communion, at the start of each decade of the rosary, and in daily prayer, usually ending at "deliver us from evil."

original.note: Latin: our Father. the name the prayer carried in the Catholic Church for centuries.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prayer everyone memorizes as kids.
what it means: a prayer that calls God by a family word and never once says I or me.
what a scholar hears: abba behind the Greek pater; the doxology absent from Matthew's earliest manuscripts; the Catholic Mass adding it after the priest's embolism.
